t: What ESD Is and Why It Kills PC Components
title: What ESD Is and Why It Kills PC Components
description: Electrostatic discharge is the spark you feel touching a doorknob in winter — thousands of volts from a charge your body picked up walking across carpet. Modern CPUs, RAM, and GPUs use transistors so small that a discharge you cannot even feel can punch through their gate oxides and kill them silently. An ESD-safe workstation drains that charge away continuously, so components never see the spike. This is why every serious build bench has ESD protection.

demo.program:
# Human-body model: walking on carpet can charge you to ~35,000 V.
# A discharge you FEEL is ~3,000 V; damage to chips starts near ~100 V.
felt_v, damage_v = 3000, 100
print(f"Felt threshold: {felt_v} V | chip damage threshold: ~{damage_v} V")
print("Conclusion: you can kill a CPU with a discharge you never feel.")
print("Fix: continuous drain via ESD mat + wrist strap.")

t: How an ESD Mat Drains Charge: Dissipative Surfaces
title: How an ESD Mat Drains Charge: Dissipative Surfaces
description: An ESD mat is made from a dissipative material — not a conductor, not an insulator, but in between, with surface resistivity typically between 10^6 and 10^9 ohms per square. Charge flows across it slowly and evenly to a ground snap instead of sparking. The mat covers the bench where parts rest, and a coiled cord ties its ground snap to a common ground point, giving every component a single quiet path to earth.

demo.program:
r_low, r_high = 1e6, 1e9
print(f"Dissipative range: {r_low:.0e} to {r_high:.0e} ohms/square")
print("Below 1e6: too conductive (spark risk). Above 1e9: too insulating (no drain).")
print("Mat + ground cord = one quiet path to earth for every part on the bench.")

t: Mat Sizes, Layers, and What to Buy
title: Mat Sizes, Layers, and What to Buy
description: Common bench mats run 24 by 36 inches — enough for a motherboard, tools, and parts — with smaller 18 by 24 inch mats for tight desks. Two-layer mats (dissipative top over conductive bottom) drain more evenly than single-layer ones. Look for a 10 mm ground snap, a textured easy-clean top, and heat resistance if you solder nearby. Expect 25 to 60 dollars for a proper mat; the cheapest foam 'ESD' mats are often just pink plastic with no real dissipative rating.

demo.program:
mats = [("18x24 in single-layer", 18, "tight desks, light use"),
        ("24x36 in two-layer", 45, "standard build bench"),
        ("36x48 in two-layer", 70, "server / dual-system benches")]
for name, price, use in mats:
    print(f"  {name:<24} ~${price:<3} {use}")
print("Check: 10mm snap, dissipative rating printed, not just pink foam.")

t: Wrist Strap Anatomy: Band, Cord, and the 1-Megohm Resistor
title: Wrist Strap Anatomy: Band, Cord, and the 1-Megohm Resistor
description: A wrist strap has three parts: an adjustable band (fabric with conductive fibers or a metal plate) that must touch bare skin, a coiled cord with a 10 mm snap, and — critically — a 1-megohm resistor built into the cord or snap. That resistor limits current if you touch live mains, so the strap protects both the component and you. The band goes on snug against skin; over a shirt sleeve it does nothing at all.

demo.program:
print("Wrist strap chain: skin -> band -> 1 Mohm resistor -> cord -> common ground")
v_fault = 120
i = v_fault / 1e6
print(f"If you touch {v_fault}V mains, the resistor limits current to {i*1000:.1f} mA (safe).")
print("Band must touch BARE skin. Over a sleeve = no protection.")

t: The Common Ground Point: Tying Mat, Strap, and Bench Together
title: The Common Ground Point: Tying Mat, Strap, and Bench Together
description: Mat and strap must share one ground — the common point ground, usually a small bar or block with multiple 10 mm snaps. The ground cord then runs to a verified earth ground (a grounded outlet's ground pin via a proper adapter, or building ground). Daisy-chaining grounds or grounding to a painted case creates multiple paths and defeats the system. One point, one path, everything bonded to it.

demo.program:
chain = ["wrist strap snap", "mat snap", "common point ground bar",
         "ground cord", "verified earth ground"]
print("Bonding chain (single path, no branches):")
for i, link in enumerate(chain, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {link}")
print("Never: daisy-chained cords, painted surfaces, ungrounded 'ground' adapters.")

t: Setting Up a Complete ESD-Safe Build Bench
title: Setting Up a Complete ESD-Safe Build Bench
description: Lay the mat flat on the bench with the snap at the back edge, plug the mat's ground cord into the common point, and snap the wrist strap cord to the same point. Put on the strap before touching any component, and keep parts on the mat — not on the bare bench or on anti-static bags' outsides (only the insides are dissipative). Test the strap with a wrist-strap tester before each build session; a dead strap looks identical to a live one.

demo.program:
steps = ["mat flat, snap at back", "mat cord -> common point",
         "strap on BARE wrist", "strap cord -> common point",
         "parts live ON the mat only", "test strap before each session"]
for i, s in enumerate(steps, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")
print("Anti-static bag outsides are NOT dissipative - keep parts inside or on the mat.")

t: ANSI/ESD S20.20: The Standard Behind the Gear
title: ANSI/ESD S20.20: The Standard Behind the Gear
description: ANSI/ESD S20.20 is the industry standard for ESD control programs, used by electronics manufacturers worldwide. It requires wrist straps to test under 35 megohms system resistance, worksurfaces under 10^9 ohms, and a documented control plan with regular verification. You do not need certification for a home bench, but buying gear rated to S20.20 means it was tested to real numbers instead of marketing claims.

demo.program:
print("ANSI/ESD S20.20 key numbers:")
print("  wrist strap system: < 35 Mohm")
print("  worksurface: < 1e9 ohm")
print("  verification: documented, on a schedule")
print("Home bench: buy S20.20-rated gear, test strap each session.")

t: Testing Your Strap and Mat: What Passes and What Fails
title: Testing Your Strap and Mat: What Passes and What Fails
description: A wrist-strap tester checks the whole skin-to-ground path in one second: green means under the limit, red means the band, cord, or resistor has failed. Test by pressing the plate while wearing the strap. Mats get checked with a surface resistivity meter — readings between 10^6 and 10^9 ohms per square pass. Cords fail most often at the snap joint from repeated flexing; replace cords yearly on a busy bench.

demo.program:
print("Wrist strap tester: press plate while wearing strap")
print("  GREEN (<35 Mohm system): pass, build away")
print("  RED: fail - check band contact, then cord, then replace")
print("Mat resistivity meter: 1e6-1e9 ohm/sq = pass")
print("Most common failure: cord snap joint (flex fatigue) - replace yearly.")

t: Use Case: Handling a CPU and RAM Safely
title: Use Case: Handling a CPU and RAM Safely
description: CPUs and RAM are the most ESD-sensitive parts in a build. The safe sequence: strap on and tested, open the motherboard box on the mat, ground yourself by touching the mat, then lift the CPU by its edges and seat it without touching the gold pads. RAM goes from its anti-static bag straight to the mat, then into the slot by its edges. Never walk across carpet carrying a CPU — sit down, stay strapped, handle parts at the bench.

demo.program:
seq = ["strap on + tested", "parts staged ON the mat", "touch mat to equalize",
       "lift CPU/RAM by EDGES only", "seat directly, no gold-pad contact"]
for i, s in enumerate(seq, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")
print("Never carry a CPU across carpet unstrapped.")

t: Use Case: GPU Installs and Long Build Sessions
title: Use Case: GPU Installs and Long Build Sessions
description: GPUs are big, expensive, and handled for minutes at a time — prime ESD victims. Keep the strap on for the whole session, rest the GPU on the mat (not the desk) while routing power cables, and touch the mat before picking the card up again after any break. In dry winter air, run a humidifier near the bench: raising humidity from 20 to 45 percent cuts static generation dramatically, which is the cheapest ESD upgrade there is.

demo.program:
print("Long-session rules:")
print("  - strap stays on the whole build (not just for the CPU)")
print("  - GPU rests on the mat between steps")
print("  - touch mat after every break before touching parts")
print("  - winter: humidifier to 40-50% RH (cuts static generation sharply)")

t: Maintenance: Cleaning Mats Without Killing the Dissipative Layer
title: Maintenance: Cleaning Mats Without Killing the Dissipative Layer
description: Clean mats with a damp cloth and a cleaner rated for ESD surfaces — harsh solvents and silicone sprays coat the dissipative layer and raise its resistance into the insulating range. Never use Armor All-type dressings. Wipe in one direction, let the mat air-dry, then re-test with a resistivity meter if you have one. A mat that reads above 10^9 ohms per square after cleaning is done — replace it.

demo.program:
ok = ["damp cloth", "ESD-rated surface cleaner", "mild soap + water (rinsed)"]
bad = ["silicone sprays", "Armor All-type dressings", "harsh solvents"]
print("Safe:", ", ".join(ok))
print("Banned:", ", ".join(bad))
print("After cleaning: re-test; >1e9 ohm/sq = replace the mat.")

t: Common ESD Mistakes That Void All Your Protection
title: Common ESD Mistakes That Void All Your Protection
description: The classic mistakes: strap over a shirt sleeve, parts sitting on the bare bench instead of the mat, the mat's ground cord unplugged, standing on carpet while handling a board, and stacking anti-static bags (their outsides are insulators). Any single one breaks the chain and the whole setup is decoration. The fix is a two-second ritual: strap on skin, cord snapped, parts on mat — checked before every session.

demo.program:
mistakes = ["strap over sleeve", "parts on bare bench", "ground cord unplugged",
            "carpet + unstrapped handling", "trusting bag OUTSIDES", "never testing the strap"]
print("Chain-breakers (any one voids protection):")
for m in mistakes:
    print(f"  X {m}")
print("Ritual: skin contact, cord snapped, parts on mat - every session.")

t: ESD Mat vs Anti-Static Bag vs ESD Flooring
title: ESD Mat vs Anti-Static Bag vs ESD Flooring
description: The mat protects the bench surface where parts rest; anti-static bags protect parts in storage and transit (insides only); ESD flooring and heel straps protect people who must move around a production floor. For a home builder the mat plus wrist strap covers nearly everything, because you sit still at the bench. Bags are for storage, flooring is for factories — do not substitute one for another.

demo.program:
print("mat + wrist strap : the seated builder's workstation (covers ~everything)")
print("anti-static bags  : storage & transit (insides dissipative, outsides not)")
print("ESD flooring      : factories where people must walk while handling boards")
print("Home bench: mat + strap. Do not substitute bags or flooring for the mat.")

t: Wrist Strap Alternatives: Heel Straps, Smocks, and Continuous Monitors
title: Wrist Strap Alternatives: Heel Straps, Smocks, and Continuous Monitors
description: Heel grounders strap to the shoe and drain through ESD flooring — the choice when you must stand and move. ESD smocks with conductive threads keep clothing from generating charge. Continuous monitors watch the strap's resistance in real time and alarm the instant it fails, which factories use instead of manual testers. For home use the plain coiled-cord strap plus a tester is the sweet spot of cost and safety.

        ("ESD smock", "charge-generating clothing"),
        ("continuous monitor", "real-time strap alarm (factories)"),
        ("coiled strap + tester", "home bench sweet spot")]
for name, use in alts:
    print(f"  {name:<22} -> {use}")
